title: Chapter 86 — The Tail
paragraphs: Other poets have sung the praises of the soft eye of the antelope and the lovely plumage of the bird that never lands. Less heavenly, I celebrate a tail.

If you reckon the largest sperm whale's tail to begin at the point of the trunk where it tapers to about the girth of a man, it covers an area on its upper surface alone of at least fifty square feet. The compact round root expands into two broad, firm, flat palms or flukes, gradually thinning to less than an inch in thickness. At the junction, these flukes slightly overlap, then separate from each other like wings, leaving a wide gap between them. In no living thing are the lines of beauty more exquisitely defined than in the crescent borders of these flukes. At full expansion in a full-grown whale, the tail will considerably exceed twenty feet across.

The entire structure seems a dense, webbed bed of welded sinews. But cut into it and you find three distinct layers: upper, middle, and lower. The fibers in the upper and lower layers are long and horizontal. Those in the middle are very short, running crosswise between the outer layers. This three-part structure, as much as anything else, gives the tail its power. To the student of old Roman walls, the middle layer will offer a curious parallel to the thin course of tiles always alternating with stone in those wonderful ancient ruins, which undoubtedly contribute so much to the masonry's great strength.

But as if this vast local power in the muscular tail were not enough, the whole bulk of the leviathan is knit over with a mesh of muscular fibers and filaments. These pass on either side of the loins and run down into the flukes, blending with them seamlessly and greatly adding to their might. So in the tail, the measureless force of the whole whale seems concentrated to a point. If annihilation could occur to matter, this would be the thing to do it.

Nor does this amazing strength at all cripple the graceful flexibility of its motions, where an infantlike ease undulates through a titanic power. On the contrary, those motions derive their most awesome beauty from it. Real strength never impairs beauty or harmony but often bestows it. In everything impressively beautiful, strength has much to do with the magic. Take away the tied tendons that everywhere seem bursting from the marble in the carved Hercules, and its charm would be gone. When devout Eckermann lifted the linen sheet from Goethe's naked corpse, he was overwhelmed by the massive chest, which seemed like a Roman triumphal arch. When Michelangelo paints even God the Father in human form, mark what robustness is there. And whatever they may reveal of divine love in the Son, those soft, curled Italian paintings in which his image has been most successfully embodied — so destitute of all brawniness — hint nothing of any power but the merely passive, feminine one of submission and endurance, which by all accounts form the peculiar practical virtues of his teachings.

Such is the subtle elasticity of the organ I describe that whether wielded in sport, in earnest, or in anger, whatever its mood, its movements are invariably marked by exceeding grace. No fairy's arm can surpass it.
Five great motions are peculiar to it. First, when used as a fin for propulsion. Second, when used as a club in battle. Third, in sweeping. Fourth, in lob-tailing. Fifth, in peaking flukes.

First: Being horizontal in position, the Leviathan's tail acts differently from the tails of all other sea creatures. It never wriggles. In man or fish, wriggling is a sign of inferiority. To the whale, his tail is his sole means of propulsion. Coiled forward like a scroll beneath the body and then rapidly sprung backward — this is what gives that singular darting, leaping motion to the monster when swimming furiously. His side fins serve only to steer.

Second: It is somewhat significant that while one sperm whale fights another only with his head and jaw, in his conflicts with man he chiefly and contemptuously uses his tail. In striking at a boat, he swiftly curves his flukes away from it, and the blow is delivered only by the recoil. If made in the unobstructed air, especially if it descends on its mark, the stroke is simply irresistible. No ribs of man or boat can withstand it. Your only salvation lies in dodging it. But if it comes sideways through the water, then partly owing to the light buoyancy of the whaleboat and the springiness of its materials, a cracked rib or a smashed plank or two — a sort of stitch in the side — is generally the worst of it. These underwater side-blows are so common in the fishery that they are considered child's play. Someone strips off a shirt, and the hole is plugged.

Third: I cannot prove it, but it seems to me that in the whale the sense of touch is concentrated in the tail. In this respect, there is a delicacy in it matched only by the daintiness of the elephant's trunk. This sensitivity is chiefly shown in the action of sweeping, when with maidenly gentleness the whale slowly moves his immense flukes from side to side upon the surface of the sea. And if he feels but a sailor's whisker — woe to that sailor, whiskers and all. What tenderness there is in that preliminary touch! Had this tail any grasping power, I should think of Darmonodes' elephant that so frequented the flower market and with low bows presented bouquets to young ladies, then caressed their waists. On more accounts than one, it is a pity the whale does not possess this grasping ability. For I have heard of yet another elephant that, when wounded in a fight, curved its trunk around and extracted the dart.

Fourth: Coming upon the whale unawares in the fancied security of the open seas, you find him unbent from the vast dignity of his bulk, and kittenlike, he plays on the ocean as if it were a hearth. But still you see his power in his play. The broad palms of his tail are flipped high into the air, then brought smiting down upon the surface — the thunderous concussion resounding for miles. You would almost think a cannon had been fired. And if you noticed the light wreath of vapor from the blowhole at his other end, you would think that was the smoke from the touch-hole.

Fifth: In his normal floating posture, the leviathan's flukes lie considerably below the level of his back, completely out of sight beneath the surface. But when he is about to plunge into the depths, his entire flukes and at least thirty feet of his body are tossed erect in the air, remaining there vibrating a moment before they shoot downward out of view. Except for the sublime breach — to be described elsewhere — this peaking of the whale's flukes is perhaps the grandest sight in all of living nature. Out of the bottomless deep, the gigantic tail seems to be spasmodically grasping at the highest heaven. So in dreams, I have seen majestic Satan thrusting forth his tormented colossal claw from the flaming Baltic of Hell. But in gazing at such scenes, it all depends on your mood. If you are in the Dantean frame, devils will come to mind. If in that of Isaiah, archangels. Standing at the masthead of my ship during a sunrise that crimsoned sky and sea, I once saw a large herd of whales in the east, all heading toward the sun, and for a moment vibrating in concert with peaked flukes. As it seemed to me then, such a grand embodiment of adoration of the gods was never seen, even in Persia, the home of fire worshippers. As Ptolemy Philopater testified of the African elephant, I then testified of the whale, pronouncing him the most devout of all beings. For according to King Juba, the military elephants of antiquity often hailed the morning with their trunks uplifted in the most profound silence.

The casual comparison in this chapter between the whale and the elephant — so far as some aspects of the tail of the one and the trunk of the other are concerned — should not suggest those two organs are equal, much less the creatures they belong to. For as the mightiest elephant is but a terrier to Leviathan, so compared with Leviathan's tail, his trunk is but the stalk of a lily. The most dreadful blow from the elephant's trunk would be as the playful tap of a fan compared with the measureless crush and crash of the sperm whale's ponderous flukes, which have repeatedly hurled entire boats with all their oars and crews into the air, much as an Indian juggler tosses his balls.*

*Though all comparison in general bulk between the whale and the elephant is absurd — inasmuch as in that regard the elephant stands in much the same relation to the whale as a dog does to the elephant — nevertheless, there are some points of curious similarity. Among these is the spout. It is well known that the elephant will often draw up water or dust in his trunk, and then, elevating it, jet it forth in a stream.

The more I consider this mighty tail, the more I deplore my inability to express it. At times there are gestures in it that, though they would well grace the hand of man, remain wholly inexplicable. In an extensive herd, so remarkable are these mystic gestures that I have heard hunters declare them akin to Freemason signs and symbols — that the whale, by these methods, was intelligently conversing with the world. Nor are there lacking other motions of the whale in his general body, full of strangeness and unaccountable to his most experienced pursuer. Dissect him how I may, then, I only go skin deep. I do not know him, and never will. But if I cannot even understand the tail of this whale, how can I understand his head? Much more, how can I comprehend his face, when he has none? You shall see my back parts, my tail, he seems to say, but my face shall not be seen. But I cannot fully make out his back parts either. And hint what he will about his face — I say again he has no face.
